# **EAiSER Campus Quests: Systems Report**

## **Overview**

Campus Quests adds two big features to EAiSER at SJSU: **Lost & Found by photo**, and a **3D HUD Campus Map** of every reported problem.

•         **Lost & Found:** a student reports a lost item by uploading a picture of it and dropping an approximate pin where they lost it.  
•         **3D HUD Campus Map:** a tilted 3D model of campus with a game-style heads-up display on top. Every problem students report (slow Wi-Fi, potholes, broken water filters, overflowing trash, accessibility barriers, rats) appears as a glowing beacon, and physical obstacles such as construction zones, potholes and blocked ramps stand up out of the map as colored 3D volumes, so you can see at a glance what is in your way. Students take on doable missions from the map, like finding lost items. Anyone who returns a lost item to the campus Lost & Found office earns rewards toward an on-campus meal voucher. The HUD also alerts students with disabilities when they walk toward an obstacle and draws the detour.

EAiSER already handles routing: every report it triages goes straight to the right campus authority. Our features sit on top of that, so the team builds the student experience, not the routing.

The loop: a student reports → EAiSER triages and routes it → a pin appears on the map → the authority fixes it or a student completes a mission → the reporter is notified and the helper is rewarded.

## **Users and roles**

Six roles share the system, and one person can hold several. Students and staff sign in with an SJSU email.

| Role | Who | What they do |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Reporter | Any student or staff member | Reports problems and lost items, tracks their status |
| Helper | Any student | Takes missions from the map, brings found items to Lost & Found, earns rewards |
| Accessibility user | A student who opts in | Gets phone alerts near construction zones, potholes and other barriers |
| Campus authorities | Whoever EAiSER routes a report to (Facilities, IT, Grounds, Housing) | Receive and fix reports. EAiSER handles this, outside our build |
| Lost & Found office | The campus lost & found desk | Checks in returned items (which triggers the reward), releases items to their owners |
| Moderator | Project team or Student Affairs staff | Reviews mission proof, handles disputes and abuse |

## **Feature 1: Lost & Found by photo**

Reporting a lost item takes one photo and one pin. Every found item ends up at the campus Lost & Found office, where the owner picks it up and the finder gets credit for the return.

**Reporting a lost item**

1\.       Upload a picture of the item: your own photo of it, or a similar image if you don't have one (for example, the product photo of the same water bottle).  
2\.       Drop an approximate pin, or circle the area, where you think you lost it. Optionally add a time window ("between 2 and 4 PM").  
3\.       EAiSER's image AI fills in the details: category, color, brand and visible marks such as stickers or a phone case. The student only confirms them, so the whole report takes under 30 seconds.

**Reporting a found item**

The finder snaps a photo and pins where they found it. They then either bring it to the Lost & Found office or leave a delivery mission for another student to carry it there.

**Matching**

The AI compares each found item with open lost reports on four signals: photo similarity, category, distance between pins and time. A strong match notifies the owner: "Possible match for your AirPods case. It's at the Lost & Found office." The owner checks the photo, then picks the item up at the office with their student ID.

**Rewards**

The finder earns points when the Lost & Found office checks the item in, by scanning a code on the finder's phone. They earn a bonus when the owner picks it up. Points add up toward an on-campus meal voucher; rates are in Feature 2\.

**Rules**

•         All handoffs go through the office, so owners and finders never have to meet or share contact details.  
•         Photos of IDs, cards and screens are auto-blurred before they appear on the map.  
•         Lost reports expire after 30 days unless the owner renews them.

**Missions it creates on the map**

•         **Search mission:** a lost report puts a mission in its area: "Keep an eye out for a black AirPods case, MLK Library floor 3."  
•         **Delivery mission:** a found item that isn't at the office yet becomes a mission to carry it there.

## **Feature 2: 3D HUD campus map**

The map is the app's home screen. It shows campus as a tilted 3D scene with a heads-up display (HUD) layered on top, like the minimap and compass in a video game. Every open report on campus is a beacon, missions are beacons that students can claim, and obstacles stand up out of the ground as 3D shapes, so a student can tell from across the quad that the Clark Hall entrance is blocked.

**The 3D scene**

•         **Campus in 3D:** the camera is tilted about 60° over a dark, low-contrast base map. SJSU buildings are extruded to their real heights from OpenStreetMap and drawn in muted gray, so the colored reports stand out. Students drag to pan, use two fingers to rotate and tilt, and tap a compass button to snap back to north-up.  
•         **Report beacons:** each report is a thin glowing column colored by category. The column is taller for higher severity and for more "Me too" votes, so the biggest problems are visible from far away. Missions get a floating points badge on top ("+50").  
•         **Obstacle volumes:** pins in the Paths and roads and Accessibility categories are drawn as 3D shapes that match the real footprint of the problem, not as dots:

| Obstacle | How it looks in 3D |
| :---- | :---- |
| Construction zone | A see-through block, about 4 m tall, covering the closed area, with amber walls and a pulsing ring on the ground |
| Pothole or cracked sidewalk | A short red cylinder sunk into the path, with a warning ring |
| Blocked ramp or broken door button | A red barrier wall across the entrance it blocks |
| Broken elevator | A red marker on the building, labeled with the floor ("Elevator out, floors 2–5") |
| Blocked route | The affected path segment turns red. The detour is drawn as an animated cyan line |

•         **Color code:** red means it blocks the route (impassable for a wheelchair), amber means use caution, cyan is a detour or information, green is resolved. Every obstacle also has an icon and a text label, so color is never the only signal.  
•         **Privacy:** lost item reports appear as a soft 50 m circle on the ground, never a point.

**The HUD layer**

The HUD is flat, always on screen and sits on top of the 3D scene.

•         **Compass strip** (top): a heading bar like a game compass. Obstacles and missions ahead show up as icons on the strip with their distance ("⚠ 120 m"), so students know what is in front of them before they see it on the map.  
•         **Status corner** (top left): points balance, active mission with its claim countdown, and a "LIVE · 23 open reports" indicator.  
•         **Ahead card** (bottom): the nearest obstacle within 150 m on the student's path, with a distance that counts down as they walk and a "Show detour" button.  
•         **Filter chips** (right side): category, status and distance. Hidden categories fade out of the 3D scene.  
•         **Proximity mode:** within 150 m of an obstacle, its 3D volume pulses, the screen edge glows amber, the Ahead card slides up, the phone vibrates (where supported) and, for low-vision users, the alert is read aloud.

**Built for accessibility, too**

•         The accessibility profile decides what counts as an obstacle for each student. A wheelchair user sees stairs, broken elevators and blocked ramps in red; obstacles that don't affect them are dimmed rather than hidden.  
•         A "2D" toggle switches to a flat top-down map for screen readers, older phones and anyone who prefers it. The app respects the phone's reduced-motion and high-contrast settings.  
•         Every pin and alert has a text version that screen readers can announce.

**What appears on the map**

Every report EAiSER has triaged appears as a beacon, colored by category. Tapping a beacon opens a sheet that shows what was reported, its status, and which authority EAiSER routed it to. Our app never picks the department.

| Category | Example reports | What students can do |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Connectivity | Slow Wi-Fi in a study room | Verify with an in-app speed test at the pin |
| Water | Broken or red-light bottle filler | Verify with a photo |
| Waste | Overflowing trash, litter | Quick tidy of litter. Overflowing bins go to staff |
| Paths and roads | Potholes, cracked sidewalks, construction | Nothing to fix. These trigger accessibility alerts |
| Accessibility | Broken elevator, blocked ramp, broken door button | Check whether it's still blocked. These trigger alerts |
| Pests | Rats, insects | Report only. Never a mission |
| Lost & Found | Lost items, found items | Search and delivery missions |

Filters cover category, status and distance. A "Me too" button on any pin merges duplicate reports and raises the report's priority.

**How a report becomes a mission**

Every report is stored with a fix\_path tag that decides what the map does with it:

•         staff: EAiSER routes it to an authority. The pin can be viewed but not claimed.  
•         self\_fixable: the issue type is on an allowlist, severity is low and no hazard flag is set (electrical, chemical, biohazard, pests, broken glass, heights, restricted areas). The pin becomes a mission, and the report still goes to the authority.  
•         lost\_found: the item enters matching and creates search or delivery missions.

Moderators can override the tag. Every override is logged so the allowlist can be tuned.

**Missions**

| Mission | Example | Proof | Points (proposed) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Return a found item | Carry a found water bottle to the Lost & Found office | Office check-in scan | 50 \+ 25 when the owner picks it up |
| Search for a lost item | Look for a lost AirPods case on MLK Library floor 3 | A found report that matches it | Same as a return, once it's checked in |
| Accessibility check | Is the ramp at the Engineering building still blocked? | A geotagged photo at the pin | 10 |
| Verify a report | Is the Wi-Fi still slow on MLK floor 4? Is the filler still broken? | Speed test or photo at the pin | 5 |
| Quick tidy | Pick up litter or return chairs to a study room | Before and after photos | 10 |

**Claiming a mission**

•         Tap a pin to see the task, points and proof needed, then tap Claim.  
•         The mission is locked to that student for 30 minutes, then reopens if no proof arrives.  
•         The mission tracker shows active and completed missions, points that are pending and spendable, and progress toward the next meal voucher.

**Points and rewards**

•         Points land as *pending*, then become *spendable* after verification, or after 24 hours with no dispute.  
•         Proposed rate: 100 points \= \$5 campus meal credit, with a weekly cap of 300 points per student. The cap bounds the reward budget.  
•         Redemption creates a one-time code that campus dining scans at checkout.  
•         Light motivation on top: streaks, badges ("Returned 5 items") and a building-vs-building leaderboard.

**Accessibility alerts**

A student with a disability who opts in gets a phone alert when they walk toward a construction zone, a pothole or another obstacle on the map. The alert says what is ahead, gives a detour and estimates the delay, and the HUD shows it in 3D: the obstacle pulses, the Ahead card counts down the distance and the detour line lights up.

•         **What triggers alerts:** pins in the Paths and roads and Accessibility categories, such as construction zones, potholes, broken elevators and blocked ramps. A student-reported pin starts alerting once staff confirm it or 3 students tap "Me too".  
•         **Who gets them:** students who turn alerts on in a private profile and choose their needs (wheelchair or scooter, crutches or a temporary injury, low vision, avoiding stairs). No documentation is required, and the profile is never shown to anyone.  
•         **How an alert fires:** the phone watches geofences around the nearest relevant pins (iOS allows 20 at a time, refreshed as the student moves). Within 150 m it shows a notification such as "Construction ahead at the Clark Hall north entrance. Use the east ramp; adds about 4 min." Tapping it opens the 3D map, flies the camera to the obstacle and draws the detour.  
•         **In the hackathon build:** the app is a mobile web app, so alerts fire while it is open. The phone's GPS position is checked against obstacle footprints every few seconds, and the alert appears in the HUD with vibration (Android) and a spoken message. A "Simulate walk" button moves the student's dot along a preset path toward the construction zone, so the alert fires reliably on stage. Background geofencing in native apps comes later.  
•         **Keeping it accurate:** each alert has a "Still blocked?" yes/no button, and accessibility check missions confirm or clear pins. Each pin alerts a student at most once per day, and alerts work with screen readers and vibration.

## **Architecture**

EAiSER does the triage and routing: it reads each photo, names the issue and sends it to the right authority. Our backend stores the result, sets fix\_path and runs everything students see: the map, missions, matching, rewards and alerts.

![System architecture · 2 clients, 4 backend services, 4 dependencies][image1]

System architecture · 2 clients, 4 backend services, 4 dependencies

All four backend services read from and write to the same Postgres database; the drawing pairs each one with the dependency it relies on most. Realtime subscriptions on reports and missions push new beacons and obstacles into every open 3D map without a refresh.

For the hackathon, the student app and the office/moderator console are one mobile-first web app with separate screens. It opens in a phone browser and can be added to the home screen, which saves building native iOS and Android apps.

**Hackathon stack** (free tiers, no app store)

| Piece | Tool | Why |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| App | Next.js (React) \+ Tailwind CSS, deployed on Vercel | One codebase for the student app, office console and API routes |
| 3D map | MapLibre GL JS with the free OpenFreeMap "Liberty" style | No API key; the style already includes 3D building extrusions for campus |
| Obstacle shapes | MapLibre fill-extrusion and line layers fed by GeoJSON, plus turf.js for circles, buffers and distances | 3D volumes without a game engine |
| HUD | Plain React components positioned over the map | Compass strip, Ahead card and status corner are ordinary UI |
| Database, auth, photos, live updates | Supabase (Postgres \+ PostGIS, Storage, Realtime) | One service covers four backend needs |
| Triage AI | EAiSER's API, falling back to a vision model that returns the same JSON | The demo works even if EAiSER access is delayed |
| Office check-in | QR code on the finder's phone (qrcode.react), scanned by the office screen (html5-qrcode), with a 6-digit code as backup | No hardware needed |

## **Data model**

One reports table holds every pin. Its fix\_path column decides whether a report is only shown on the map, becomes a mission, or enters lost & found matching. Points live in an append-only ledger, so every balance is the sum of its rows and can be audited.

| Table | Key fields | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| users | id, sjsu\_email, display\_name, role, banned\_at | One account per SJSU email |
| reports | id, reporter\_id, kind (issue / lost / found), category, issue\_type, severity, title, description, photo\_urls, location (lat/lng point), footprint (polygon, for obstacles that cover an area), building, floor, fix\_path (staff / self\_fixable / lost\_found), hazard\_flags, access\_impact, routed\_to (from EAiSER), status, created\_at | Every pin on the map |
| report\_votes | report\_id, user\_id | "Me too" duplicate merges |
| items | report\_id, category, color, brand, marks, image\_embedding, area (approximate circle), whereabouts (with finder / at office / picked up), office\_checkin\_at | Lost & found item details |
| matches | lost\_report\_id, found\_report\_id, score, status (suggested / confirmed / rejected) | Matching engine results |
| missions | id, report\_id, mission\_type, points, proof\_required, claimed\_by, claim\_expires\_at, status | Doable work on the map |
| mission\_proofs | mission\_id, helper\_id, photo\_urls, speed\_test, gps\_point, taken\_at, ai\_check, review\_status | Evidence for verification |
| points\_ledger | id, user\_id, delta, reason, mission\_id, state (pending / spendable / reversed), created\_at | Append-only points history |
| rewards | id, name, cost\_points, partner, stock | Meal voucher catalog |
| redemptions | id, user\_id, reward\_id, code, redeemed\_at | One-time voucher codes |
| status\_events | report\_id, from\_status, to\_status, actor\_id, at | Full status history for every report |
| access\_alerts | report\_id, affects (wheelchair / low\_vision / no\_stairs / …), obstacle\_style (zone / pothole / barrier / elevator / route), impact (blocks = red / caution = amber), label, detour\_text, detour\_path (line), blocked\_path (line), est\_delay\_min, confirmed | Obstacles that trigger accessibility alerts and how the 3D map draws them |
| access\_profiles | user\_id, needs\[\], alert\_radius\_m, travel\_speed, alerts\_on | Private opt-in settings, never shown to others |

Supabase gives us Postgres with PostGIS for queries like "missions within 300 m" and "obstacles near this student", plus realtime subscriptions so new beacons and obstacles appear live on the 3D map. The map reads reports as GeoJSON: points for beacons, footprint polygons for obstacle volumes and detour\_path lines for detours.

CREATE TYPE fix\_path AS ENUM ('staff', 'self\_fixable', 'lost\_found');

 CREATE TABLE reports (  
   id        	uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen\_random\_uuid(),  
   reporter\_id   uuid REFERENCES users(id),  
   kind      	text CHECK (kind IN ('issue', 'lost', 'found')),  
   category  	text,      	\-- connectivity, water, waste, paths, accessibility, pests, lost\_found  
   issue\_type	text,  
   severity  	smallint,  
   title     	text,  
   description   text,  
   photo\_urls	text\[\],  
   location  	geography(Point, 4326),  
   footprint 	geography(Polygon, 4326),  	\-- optional area for construction zones and other obstacles  
   building  	text,  
   fix\_path  	fix\_path NOT NULL,  
   hazard\_flags  text\[\] DEFAULT '{}',  
   access\_impact text\[\] DEFAULT '{}',  
   routed\_to 	text,      	\-- authority chosen by EAiSER  
   status    	text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'submitted',  
   created\_at	timestamptz DEFAULT now()  
 );

## **Status lifecycle**

Every report follows one of three paths after triage. All three end the same way: the reporter is notified and the pin closes.

![Report status lifecycle · 3 paths, 1 retry loop][image2]

Report status lifecycle · 3 paths, 1 retry loop

Each status change is written to status\_events, so the reporter's timeline and the moderator audit read from the same history. Points become spendable only at "Verified, paid" or "Checked in".

## **Trust, safety and anti-abuse**

Points are worth real money, so every reward needs proof that someone other than the helper can check.

**Verifying proof**

•         Proof photos must be taken in the app (no gallery uploads), within about 50 m of the pin and after the claim.  
•         An AI check compares before and after photos ("is the litter gone?"). Low-confidence results go to a moderator.  
•         A random 10% of proofs that pass also get a human review.  
•         Lost & found rewards need the Lost & Found office to check the item in, so a third party always confirms them.

**Stopping point farming**

•         Students can't claim missions on their own reports, or earn a return reward for an item they reported lost.  
•         Duplicate reports at the same pin within 24 hours merge into one mission.  
•         The weekly point cap and the 24-hour pending period limit what fraud can earn. A rejected proof reverses its pending points.  
•         Repeated rejections lead to review and possible bans. One account per SJSU email.

**Physical safety**

•         Hazards are never missions: electrical, chemical, biohazard, pests, broken glass, heights, labs, roofs and construction zones.  
•         All found items go through the Lost & Found office, so no one has to meet a stranger.  
•         Missions could be limited to daylight hours and well-lit areas. The team still has to decide this.

**Privacy**

•         Lost item pins show a 50 m area publicly, never the exact spot.  
•         Faces, ID numbers and card numbers in photos are auto-blurred before a pin goes public.  
•         Profiles show display names only, and owners and finders never need each other's contact details.  
•         Accessibility alerts run on the phone. The server sends the list of pins, the operating system's geofencing checks distance, and no location history is stored. Students can turn off or delete their accessibility profile at any time.

## **Hackathon scope and success metrics**

Build one complete loop for Saturday's 1 PM demo: report a lost item with a photo and pin → a teammate reports finding it and the app matches the two → the item is checked in on a mock Lost & Found office screen → points arrive → redeem a meal voucher code. In the same demo, open the 3D HUD map, tap "Simulate walk" toward the construction zone at Clark Hall and show the obstacle pulsing, the Ahead card counting down, the spoken alert and the cyan detour. Everything else goes in the pitch, not the build. The team split is in the roles folder: start with roles/shared.md, then each person's own file.

| Area | Demo build (by Sat 1 PM) | Later |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Intake | Photo \+ pin through EAiSER triage, plus the fix\_path rules | Model-based tagging tuned from moderator overrides |
| Lost & Found | Lost report by photo and pin, found report, matching by category \+ distance \+ photo, office check-in screen | Owner pickup flow, real office integration |
| Map | 3D campus with extruded buildings, category beacons, 3D obstacle volumes, HUD (compass strip, status corner, Ahead card, filter chips), 2D toggle, live updates, Claim button | Clustering, heatmaps, indoor 3D floor maps, AR camera view |
| Missions | Return and search missions, 30-minute claim lock | Verify, accessibility check and tidy missions, streaks, leaderboards |
| Rewards | Points ledger, mock voucher catalog, redemption code | Real dining partner, budget dashboard |
| Accessibility alerts | A construction zone, a pothole, a blocked ramp and a broken elevator drawn in 3D; a proximity alert in the HUD on a real phone (on-screen, vibration, spoken); a hand-drawn detour line; a "Simulate walk" button for the stage | Background geofencing in native apps, automatic detour routing, obstacles created straight from reports, schedule-based checks |
| Proof | Geotagged in-app photo, moderator approve button | AI before/after check, random audits |

**Success metrics for a pilot**

•         Median time from a lost report to the item being checked in at Lost & Found (goal: under 48 hours)  
•         Share of lost reports that end with the owner picking up the item  
•         Share of missions completed within 24 hours  
•         Weekly active reporters and helpers, and how many come back the next week  
•         How useful accessibility users rate the alerts, and false alerts per week  
•         Cost per returned item (vouchers paid ÷ items returned)

**Open questions**

•         Who funds the meal vouchers: Associated Students, campus dining or a sponsor?  
•         Will the Lost & Found office scan app check-ins, and what are its hours?  
•         Do OpenStreetMap's building heights look right for SJSU, or should we hand-set heights for the buildings in the demo (MLK Library, Clark Hall, Engineering, Student Union)?
